articles.title: Ferrari back Frederic Vasseur as F1 team principal
articles.summary: Ferrari back Frederic Vasseur as their F1 team principal after former Red Bull boss Christian Horner says he would be interested in joining.
articles.body:
Ferrari have backed Frederic Vasseur as their Formula 1 team principal.

The official statement comes amid speculation over the Frenchman's position, fuelled by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner saying he would be interested , external in joining Ferrari.

Ferrari chief communication officer Maria Conti used a hastily convened media call to deliver the message, saying she was speaking on behalf of chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna.

"Ferrari's position is clear," Conti said. "It will not change. l am officially saying - I don't have John here with me, but Ferrari has made its choice. There is confidence in Fred and his team. Nothing has changed."

Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A

Horner a distraction for Ferrari, says Vasseur

Ferrari entered the 2026 season hoping their preparations for widespread rule changes covering cars and engines would give them a chance to become championship contenders.

But, although their chassis started the season regarded as the best in F1, their engine has fallen short of the performance set by Mercedes and Red Bull.

Ferrari are second in the constructors' championship after 15 of a scheduled 23 races, but a massive 160 points behind leaders Mercedes and more concerned about fending off a challenge from McLaren, who are 72 points adrift in third place.

On Saturday after the race Lewis Hamilton was asked whether he was still confident Ferrari were heading in the right direction under Vasseur. He replied: "Yes."

Vasseur said after the race in Baku in reference to speculation about his future: "We are not working in the perfect serenity. For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, it's a bit of a frustrating situation.

"We are fighting for P2 in the championship, and at the end of the day we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have.

"But it is what it is - it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere.

"But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated."

Vasseur signed a new contract with Ferrari in July last year. Ferrari did not say how long it lasted beyond describing it as "a multi-year contract for the coming Formula 1 seasons".

Vasseur joined Ferrari at the start of 2023 after former team principal Mattia Binotto was removed following a bright start to the previous regulation set in 2022 was followed by a slump marked by poor reliability and questionable operational decisions.

articles.title: Frederic Vasseur: Ferrari state 'full confidence' in F1 team principal after Christian Horner comments and speculation
articles.summary: Ferrari deliver message backing Frederic Vasseur in a hastily convened media call to allow them full focus on racing on the next race and not "gossip"; watch Formula 1's return to Malaysia live on Sky Sports F1 from Friday morning as Sepang hosts the Bahrain Grand Prix
articles.body:
Vasseur admitted after last Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix that the team were "not working in perfect serenity" amid persistent and "frustrating" rumours around his position at the Scuderia.

That was amplified last week by an interview with Horner published in The Times in which the former Red Bull team principal said Ferrari were the only outfit he would consider returning to the pit-wall for without the ownership stake that he has been prioritising for any comeback to the sport.

In the unusual step of a hastily arranged media briefing on Tuesday morning ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, a Ferrari spokeswoman made clear the company had full confidence in Vasseur to continue running their F1 operation.

"Ferrari's position is clear and unchanged," said the spokesperson.

"Ferrari has made its choices and has full confidence in the leadership of Fred Vasseur and his team and we will continue to do so.

"Ferrari has always attracted interest, it's a reflection of what Ferrari represents. We say this today because we want to avoid gossip and speculation in Malaysia and focus on the weekend."

The spokesperson said the team's statement was responding to "not only the piece with Mr Horner in The Times but subsequent stories that have been increasing, not dying down".

Vasseur is in his fourth season in charge since joining from Sauber from the start of 2023 and signed a multi-year contract extension last year.

Asked if Vasseur retained the full support of Ferrari chair John Elkann and chief executive Benedetto Vigna and would stay in post for the remainder of his contract, the spokesperson reiterated: "Ferrari's position is clear and unchanged.

"Ferrari has made its choices, it has confidence in Fred Vasseur and we continue to do so."

What's left for Ferrari to play for in 2026?

After a poor 2025 season for Ferrari, when they failed to win a race and slipped to fourth place in the Constructors' Championship, Vasseur has led them back to race-winning ways this year with two victories and they sit second in the Constructors' Championship.

But the Italian team's world championship challenge to Mercedes has faded in recent months and they have not finished on the podium in the last five races.

Lewis Hamilton is third in the Drivers' Championship behind Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell and all but ruled out his title hopes after Ferrari's home Italian Grand Prix earlier in September, when he finished sixth.

Last week, Charles Leclerc and Hamilton finished fourth and sixth respectively in Baku, as the team slipped 160 points behind championship leaders Mercedes, although third-placed McLaren's failure to score any points meant Ferrari re-extended their advantage over the reigning champions to 72 points.

Ferrari have a scheduled eight races left to at least maintain their current championship positions, with Hamilton having insisted last week that a top-three finish in the drivers' would still represent a "huge achievement" for them given their troubles last season.

articles.title: Fernando Alonso says 'I still feel as fast as anybody' as he confirms he will stay in F1 in 2027 with Aston Martin
articles.summary: Fernando Alonso commits to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year. - and explains why to BBC Sport.
articles.body:
Fernando Alonso has committed to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year - and says the biggest single reason for his decision is because he "still feels fast".

The 45-year-old Spaniard has been weighing up his future all year. And while, like Max Verstappen, he has been outspoken in his criticism of the new hybrid engines introduced in 2026, his love for the sport has won out.

"First, this is my life," Alonso told BBC Sport in his only English language interview about his decision, which was announced on Tuesday. , external

"I have this in my blood and I keep racing and I keep enjoying and this is a way of life, in a way.

"Probably for me the biggest, or the clearest thing to keep racing is I still feel self-confidence that I have something extra.

"And when I think about stepping down or taking a different role in the team or not driving the car or whatever, in a way I feel it should not be like that because I still feel as fast as anybody. So let's have another go."

His own personal performance was only one factor at play in Alonso's decision, he explained in an extensive and open conversation.

Alonso also considered the new rules, and the competitiveness of his team, which has been close to rock bottom for most of this season.

'I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous'

Alonso is regarded as one of the all-time F1 greats, and has created an iconic status over a career that dates back to 2001.

And he continues to reject any suggestion that he has lost any of his ability.

"When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," Alonso says.

"I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them.

"So when I get changed and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive.

"How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch from my living room the race.

"At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that."

Alonso has only had a couple of chances this year to prove his point that he's still as good as he ever was. One was at the Dutch Grand Prix, when he finished ninth, holding at bay the faster cars of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

I suggest to him that it was a typical Alonso drive, proof to those who doubted that he still has it. But he says it will have had no impact on the audience.

"You only prove to people when you are in the podium or you are on TV," he says. "That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid.

"So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast.

"We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth and that will be a surprise for everybody again."

Carrying on despite his dislike of modern F1 cars

Along with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Alonso has been one of the drivers most critical of the 2026 rules.

Drivers feel the new hybrid engines, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have diminished F1's challenge.

The key problems are the fact the cars run out of half their energy long before some corners, a process known as "derating", and that some of the sport's most demanding corners have been neutered because they are used to charge the batteries.

Alonso, as is his way, has produced some particularly pithy turns of phrase this season to express his unhappiness.

He has called F1 the "battery world championship". He has described fast corners as "the charging station for the car" and said that "the chef could drive the car" in a particular corner in Bahrain that used to be a major challenge.

And he's been dismissive of the increased number of overtaking moves created by offsets in energy levels between cars, calling them "avoidance actions".

How did he square all that with deciding to keep racing these cars he dislikes so much?

"That's a good question," he says, "because that was the hardest thing for me."

He says he hopes the changes being made to change the power ratio to 60-40 in two steps by 2028 "will make things a little bit easier".

"This year, there have been some good races and some bad races," Alonso says. "Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving.

"And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that.

"Maybe even for next year they can tweak a little bit the battery power to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving.

"Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight, it goes against the driver instinct of braking late and going on power earlier. It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you ended up going slower and that's not the way it should be."

Alonso says that, as something of an elder statesman, he "feels some responsibility also in this regard to help the sport" make the right decisions for the future.

And the willingness of governing body the FIA and commercial rights holder F1 to accept there is a problem and make changes to address it has also been a reassurance.

"It does help that the sport keeps chasing ideas and talking to the drivers and the teams (about) how to make things better, even for the next set of regulations," he says.

"This gives me also some hope that I will enjoy more the driving next year than I did this year."

It has been a dismal year for Aston Martin, whose car has been uncompetitive, while Honda's engine has been the worst in the field on the Japanese manufacturer's official return to F1.

But a massive update to the car for the Hungarian Grand Prix cut something like two seconds off lap times, offering hope for next season.

A key influence in Alonso's decision was Adrian Newey, whose arrival as managing technical partner in March 2025 delayed the start of work on this year's car, the first of a cascading series of issues that led to this year's performance.

Alonso has been waiting his entire career to work with the man regarded as the greatest technical mind of his generation, perhaps ever. So giving up after just one, highly compromised, year together felt senseless.

"This team has all the ingredients to have success in the future," Alonso says, "and I didn't feel that this was the moment to leave. It was the moment to keep on going, giving a second chance to Honda as well to fix their problems as well and stay together with the team.

"Adrian was probably the biggest contributor to this. We didn't start it right this year but things are moving in the right direction and he's capable of changing things very quickly.

"Aston is my family. I know Lawrence (Stroll, the owner) and Lance (Stroll, Alonso's team-mate) for many, many years. We keep open conversations, many different topics, every week. And that will be the case also for next year."

Honda's engine upgrade, which debuted at the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August, was not especially convincing.

Alonso has bad memories of Honda from his time with McLaren from 2015-17, and he admits living through a similar experience again "has been difficult".

But major steps have been taken to address the internal issues at the company and Alonso says: "They are moving in the right direction. There are no guarantees that next year the engine will be completely fixed but all the changes that are happening in Honda made sense, so I have faith.

"The trust that I have in the team, it didn't change even throughout this difficult year. In the future, I don't know how long it's going to take, but it will be a successful team, and I want to be part of it."

There was one final factor - family. Alonso became a father this year when his partner, the Spanish television presenter Melissa Jimenez, gave birth to their son, Leonard, in March.

Has that had any effect on his approach to life and his career?

"I would say not," Alonso says. "I was (initially) thinking yes, and I tried to think about, family first, what will be the best for my son next year if I have this tight calendar or not and things like that.

"But then quickly I realised that it was not really a key factor. This year it was difficult for him to travel; he's only six months old now. But I think next year he will come to 50% of the races or more.

"So I could even enjoy my life more, travelling around the world with my son. That's a huge privilege that I will hopefully enjoy next year.

"Racing next year, it was my natural, final decision. I will be racing in any car, even when I stop Formula 1, but F1 is still in my blood.

"One more year made all the sense in the world for now."

"I see that it would not be only one year, but I don't have any pressure to think about it."

articles.title: Fernando Alonso renueva con Aston Martin y seguirá en la Fórmula 1
articles.standfirst: El asturiano termina con la especulación justo antes del Gran Premio de Bahréin y seguirá confiando en el proyecto del equipo británico
articles.summary: El asturiano termina con la especulación justo antes del Gran Premio de Bahréin y seguirá confiando en el proyecto del equipo británico
articles.body: Fin de los rumores y de las dudas: Fernando Alonso (julio de 1981, Oviedo) seguirá siendo piloto de Fórmula 1. El bicampeón asturiano (2005 y 2006 con Renault) competirá más cursos en la clase reina tras ampliar su vinculación como piloto (no iba a romper su vínculo con la marca) de Aston Martin. Su carrera, que inició allá por 2001 en un modesto Minardi que bastante tenía con arrancar, pasó por McLaren o Ferrari y jamás se ha puesto en duda, seguirá en la máxima categoría. Con el sueño que no ha cambiado de volver a lo más alto. Seguirá en la competición principal con un contrato multianual. Han corrido ríos de tinta hasta que el momento llegó. El de Alonso y su anuncio, que pasó por momentos de dudas ("quizá es mi última carrera en España", dijo en Madrid), otros de esperanza ("si renuevo quizá lo haré por muchos años", admitió) y una decisión en firme de seguir liderando a un proyecto que le necesita. Nada ha salido como debería en Aston Martin y el asturiano es su realidad más clara. El piloto que eleva el listón, aporta los resultados y persigue desde su cambio a equipo ganador desde 2023, año en el que aterrizó procedente de Alpine. También como baluarte del deporte, pues está en la mesa de los más grandes de todos los tiempos. Aunque eso no asegura ganar, en la F1 hay más cosas que demostrar y muchas tienen que ver con la mecánica. Esa oficialidad también tuvo su dosis de drama. Aston Martin lanzó en sus redes sociales una silla con un foco, el piloto lo compartió y a las 13:00 horas se comunicó que seguiría en la F1. "Estoy muy feliz por firmar mi nuevo contrato. Me ha llevado un tiempo, pero las carreras son mi vida, mi pasión y sé que tengo la velocidad y determinación para competir al máximo nivel", comunicó. La renovación de Alonso es, al 100%, la confirmación de la fe del piloto de Oviedo en Aston. Siempre ha repetido que cuentan con la mejor fábrica y que sólo es cuestión de tiempo el poder alcanzar la cima. Quizá el gran salto aerodinámico de Hungría ya le indicó que el buen camino va alcanzándose, aunque quedan todas las dudas relacionadas con Honda. Su motor no ha funcionado, es la realidad. Pero si el piloto sigue, no será para volver a cerrar parrillas. Y si ocurre, algo habrá fallado de nuevo. Al mismo tiempo, Alonso también había defendido que su renovación iba relacionada al estado de la F1 actual. Nunca le ha gustado. Y siempre ha sido duro. "Se han matado circuitos", señaló. Pero hay ajustes encima de la mesa y conversaciones con la FIA que pueden ir por un camino que al piloto más veterano de la parrilla le agrade. Para acercarse a unas carreras más naturales, por encima de todo, y para que la competitividad de su proyecto, especialmente en el lado de Honda, sea otra. "Me comprometo con este equipo a largo plazo para ayudarle a alcanzar el éxito. Creo sinceramente en lo que estamos construyendo: un liderazgo fuerte, gente increíble, compañeros e instalaciones", enumeró el asturiano. Como él, Lance Stroll también seguirá. Aunque en el caso del canadiense no era necesario.... Como ocurre en la F1 moderna, Alonso no especifica fechas ni límites de su vinculación. "Quiero seguir creando memorias en frente de los fans, su energía es lo que me inspira y lo hace especial", cerró en su mensaje. En su equipo, el objetivo está claro. "Estamos aquí para ganar y en nuestra lista de deseos a corto plazo queremos seguir mejorando. Tenemos dos pilotos de clase mundial que necesitamos para alcanzar nuestros objetivos", concluyó Lawrence Stroll, gran jefe de la estructura. Se apoyará en el lápiz de Newey, que funcionó con el primer gran paquete de mejoras, y un motor sobre el que siguen depositando fe. Dicen que Honda siempre termina llegando, aunque el tiempo, en este caso, es un asunto clave y que juega en contra de Alonso. Con 440 Grandes Premios y 45 años, es ley de vida. Y en el futuro siguen otros retos como las 500 Millas de Indianápolis, las 24 Horas de Le Mans o el regreso al Rally Dakar.

articles.title: Fernando Alonso: Aston Martin confirm unchanged line-up for 2027 F1 season with Spaniard and Lance Stroll extending contracts
articles.summary: Fernando Alonso will race on in F1 past at least his 46th birthday after agreeing an extended deal at Aston Martin; Alonso and Lance Stroll stay in tandem for fifth season; watch Formula 1's return to Malaysia live on Sky Sports from Friday as Sepang hosts the Bahrain GP
articles.body:
The 45-year-old will continue to race alongside team-mate Lance Stroll, whose own extended deal has also been confirmed.

Alonso, the two-time world champion from 2005-2006, will prolong his career into a record-extending 24th campaign since first racing in the sport as a 19-year-old in 2001. He has raced in 440 grands prix, winning 32, and turns 46 next July.

Aston Martin have endured a torrid first year under F1's new technical regulations in 2026, their first as Honda's works engine partners and with an Adrian Newey-led car design, scoring just three points in 15 races so far.

But the veteran Alonso, who has also been heavily critical of the sport's current engine rules, says he wants to continue on as he feels both fast enough and is "committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed".

"I'm very happy to sign a new contract with the Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team," said Alonso, who joined them from Alpine in 2023.

"I took my time to make this decision, but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level. I'm committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed.

"I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities. I look forward to making more memories on the race track in front of the passionate fans.

"Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special."

Aston Martin focus on car performance with drivers unchanged

Canada's Stroll will stay alongside Alonso for a fifth season - and a ninth year at the Silverstone-based outfit overall - at the team his father Lawrence is executive chairman at and co-owns.

"I'm very happy to continue with Aston Martin Aramco for the long term," said Stroll, 27.

"I've been on this journey since the beginning and I believe we have the resources and the people to become a winning team.

"There is so much hard work going on at Silverstone with real progress being made, and the determination I see in every department is a huge motivation for me."

Lawrence Stroll remains determined to take Aston Martin to the top of the sport, and added: "Lance and Fernando have been a crucial part of our journey and we are very pleased to confirm that they will continue with us into the next chapter for the team.

"Having two drivers with their level of experience, commitment and knowledge provides tremendous value to the whole organisation.

"We are here to win, and whilst our short-term focus remains on improving performance, I believe we have the world-class talent we need to achieve our long-term objectives."

What's left open in the driver market for 2027?

An extended stay for Alonso at Aston Martin for at least an additional year had looked likely since some of the grid's other potentially-available race-winning drivers, such as Williams' Carlos Sainz, recommitted to their existing teams over the summer break.

Aston Martin's confirmation of an unchanged line-up leaves just four seats left unfilled on next year's hitherto-static grid - at Racing Bulls and Haas.

Racing Bulls are yet to confirm either of their drivers although it appears Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad are favourite to stay on.

Haas look certain to retain Oliver Bearman but Esteban Ocon's future appears likely to lie elsewhere, with F2 title leader Rafael Camara, who is backed by Ferrari, considered the front-running alternative to the experienced Frenchman.

articles.title: How Max Verstappen can disrupt Kimi Antonelli, George Russell title fight in remainder of 2026 Formula 1 season
articles.summary: Max Verstappen and Red Bull are yet to win a race in 2026 but could they create issues for Kimi Antonelli and George Russell in their title battle; watch Formula 1's return to Malaysia from Friday morning live on Sky Sports F1 as Sepang hosts the Bahrain Grand Prix
articles.body:
Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and it will be fascinating to see how the Italian responds following what he called his "worst weekend" of the season last time out in Baku.

Depending on the quality of Mercedes' major upgrade package that will be introduced in Malaysia this week, we could see the Silver Arrows dominate the last third of the season.

However, there's one driver everyone on the grid mentions every weekend when it comes to who could challenge, or who will be a threat - and that's Max Verstappen.

This year is the first season Verstappen has not challenged for the title since 2020, having won four championships in a row from 2021 to 2024 and coming just two points short of an incredible comeback in 2025 to defeat Lando Norris.

After a difficult start to 2026, Red Bull appear to be on an upward trajectory again and history shows Verstappen will be an issue for other title protagonists.

Ten years ago, Nico Rosberg and Lewis Hamilton were duking it out for the title and Rosberg just came out on top.

It was an incredible, tense ending to the season but during the run-in, despite Mercedes having a dominant car, a 19-year-old Verstappen gave Rosberg and Hamilton a headache on a few occasions.

"My god, having him around in the races! The risk of a DNF for myself, it increases like 10-fold," Rosberg told Sky Sports F1 when reflecting on 2016.

"On my way to the championship, I had him around me every race in the last four races. He passed me I think in three of those four races, in a tussle."

At the Japanese Grand Prix, Verstappen found himself ahead of Hamilton in the closing stages and was prepared to defend aggressively in their fight for second to the frustration of the British driver.

Hamilton claimed Verstappen "moved under braking" which led to the FIA clamping down on such a manoeuvre which became known as the "Verstappen Rule".

While Brazil 2016 is remembered for Verstappen's superb comeback drive in torrential rain to the podium, he was actually running in second earlier in the race after dancing around the outside of Rosberg in Turn 3.

We are yet to have a wet race or qualifying in 2026 and, in theory, the cars with most downforce should be the best in the wet. But Verstappen's ability in the rain cannot be underestimated and he will be willing to take risks when the Mercedes drivers may not, similarly to Rosberg in 2016.

And in the season finale, Verstappen spun on the opening lap and dropped to the back but ran an alternative strategy and, in the middle of the race, had Rosberg behind him, who was on fresher tyres after pitting and needed to overtake the Red Bull driver.

"Tony [Ross, Rosberg's race engineer] saying it's critical we pass Verstappen for the championship…holy moly, seriously!" explained Rosberg.

"The feelings that I had in the battle and right after when I realised that I passed him, I've never had that in a race car before ever in my life."

Are Red Bull now a genuine threat to Mercedes?

Mercedes have consistently had a quick car at every race in 2026, not always the fastest, but good enough to at least fight for the win.

Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull on the other hand have been up and down - all three having clear weaknesses which makes them uncompetitive at certain tracks.

On average, Red Bull have had the fourth fastest car but Verstappen impressively has the most podiums (seven) of the non-Mercedes drivers and five of those have come in the last six rounds.

Red Bull brought their last big upgrade package of the season to Baku and both drivers were happy with the new parts, which included a new floor body, diffuser and sidepods.

Verstappen was less than two tenths from snatching victory away from Russell while Isack Hadjar finished an impressive third in his first race since the end of July - it marked the first time in over two years two Red Bull drivers have featured on the podium.

"On paper, Baku was the most favourable [track] in terms of car characteristics," said Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies.

"Equally, I think the performance we've shown in the race is giving us decent hope that we will get another couple of occasions before the end of the year.

"On top of getting a couple of other occasions to get that first win, it's also good to go on tracks where it's going to be more difficult, because it's exactly what we need to be confronted with to continue to progress."

The big test of Red Bull's upgrades will come this weekend at the Sepang International Circuit - a more traditional track with big medium to high-speed corners that tests a car's aerodynamics.

Tyre wear has been an issue for Red Bull but if their Baku upgrades have fixed that, Verstappen and Hadjar should be competitive again.

Verstappen: If opportunity to win is there, we go for it

This is a milestone Mekies alluded to earlier as Red Bull and Verstappen have won a race every year since 2016.

Verstappen will play things down about wanting to keep his streak of winning in 10 consecutive seasons (the record is 15 held by Hamilton and Michael Schumacher) alive, but surely deep down he is very keen to stand on the top step of the podium at least once this year.

"If Mercedes is bringing an upgrade and it works, then they take a step ahead, and that's not what you want. It will make it even more difficult to win," said Verstappen.

"But we'll try every single weekend and, of course, if the opportunity is there, we go for it."

Depending on how Mercedes' upgrades perform and how the Red Bull fares on more traditional circuits over the remainder of the season, it is hard to say which will be Verstappen's best chance of winning.

Las Vegas in November is very similar to Baku with low tyre degradation and long straights, while Mexico City in October will be interesting due to its high altitude and which power units perform best at 2000m above sea level. In the previous regulations, the Honda power unit was very strong at altitude.

Even if Verstappen is unable to win, he will be feisty on opening laps and Safety Car restarts, knowing he has nothing to lose against the Mercedes drivers.

Although Antonelli and Russell do not need to beat Verstappen, they must be wary when fighting the Dutchman because, as he reminded us in Baku, is unrelenting and never makes your life easy on the track.

articles.title: Álex Palou ya tiene nuevo compañero en Ganassi
articles.standfirst: El danés Christian Lundgaard es el elegido para ocupar el hueco que deja libre Scott Dixon
articles.summary: El danés Christian Lundgaard es el elegido para ocupar el hueco que deja libre Scott Dixon
articles.body: Era un secreto a voces y por fin Chip Ganassi Racing ha deshojado la margarita y ha anunciado al nuevo compañero de Álex Palou que, como se daba por hecho desde hace semanas, será el danés Christian Lundgaard. El ya ex piloto de McLaren (equipo en el que ha cuajado dos buenas temporadas) será el sucesor del mítico Scott Dixon en el Ganassi #9… y el encargado de ponerle las cosas algo más difíciles al pentacampeón español de la IndyCar. Lundgaard llega a Ganassi después de ser el mejor piloto papaya en la pasada campaña, con dos victorias que le auparon hasta el tercer puesto de la general final, por delante incluso de la estrella de McLaren, Pato O’Ward. El danés ha demostrado ser un piloto muy competitivo especialmente en pistas permanentes (la especialidad del español), pero no tanto en óvalos, algo que le ha impedido luchar por algo más en el campeonato. Eso sí, era el mejor agente libre disponible en el agitado mercado de la IndyCar 2027. A sus 25 años, Lundgaard ya suma tres triunfos, 16 podios y 21 top cinco en 87 carreras en EE.UU. Esos son los méritos que le han llevado al equipo más laureado de la historia de la competición, donde compartirá escuadra con Palou y Kyffin Simpson. “Es un honor y un privilegio unirme a CGR… y más en el coche 9, un volante tan especial”, explica un Lundgaard que sabe que ha dado el gran salto en su carrera deportiva: “Ganassi ha sido la referencia en la INDYCAR durante décadas y ahora tengo la oportunidad de formar parte de ese legado, algo para lo que he trabajado toda mi carrera. Estoy deseando empezar para luchar por victorias, títulos y las 500 Millas de Indianápolis”.

articles.title: Honda debe presentarse al 2027 con 50 CV más
articles.standfirst: Alonso renueva y le da una segunda oportunidad al motorista nipón, que, según he podido saber de fuentes muy reputadas del 'paddock', está a 70 CV de los mejores
articles.summary: Alonso renueva y le da una segunda oportunidad al motorista nipón, que, según he podido saber de fuentes muy reputadas del 'paddock', está a 70 CV de los mejores
articles.body: Fernando Alonso se queda. Gran noticia para la afición española, Aston Martin y la propia Fórmula 1. Una decisión tomada después de meses de reflexión donde sopesó en diversas ocasiones el adiós. De hecho, la primera idea antes de que comenzara el año es que esta iba a ser su última temporada. Pero, tal y como dijo en Madrid: “Si al final me quedo, también será por los aficionados, que no se merecen una despedida así”. Hungría fue clave para recuperar la confianza en Aston Martin. Y en su propia continuidad. Una evolución en la que al fin sentía que habían tomado una línea positiva con el chasis después de un comienzo desolador. Pero quedaba el tema del reglamento. Habló mucho con los responsables del deporte (con el presidente Ben Sulayem haciendo de Rey Juan Carlos al decir en Madrid que Fernando seguía), y se han comprometido a que la potencia durará más en recta y el pilotaje será bastante más natural con el reparto 60/40. Como nos ha dicho varias veces este verano, se siente fuerte, se siente fresco y con ganas de seguir compitiendo. Un mes de julio en el que vio que puede compaginar ser padre con llevar al niño a las carreras. Físicamente, los coches no son tampoco un desafío. Se puede competir perfectamente con más de 45 años. Lo único que castiga al piloto son los sacrificios de entrenamiento y de horas sin vida personal. Pero eso lo compensa con las ganas de competir. De pilotar un coche de Newey al fin con un motor de garantías. En Aston Martin saben que su chasis no es perfecto. El mayor defecto está en dos aspectos, la dificultad para meter la rueda en la ventana de trabajo a una vuelta, y el exceso de oposición al viento en recta. Pero ha mejorado mucho en carga aerodinámica y estabilidad. Y si no lo han mejorado más es por emplear dinero en el monoplaza del año que viene. Como resulta evidente, el punto negro es el motor. Según he podido saber de fuentes reputadas del paddock, el propulsor Honda está a 70 CV de los mejores. A dos segundos por vuelta en Baku de Mercedes. Con esos CV a su espalda estaría luchando por meterse en Q3. Lo triste es que sigan tan lejos después de poner toda la carne en el asador con la evolución de Zandvoort, y sólo mejorar un par de décimas por vuelta. El asturiano le ha dado una segunda oportunidad al fabricante nipón. Confía en su capacidad industrial para enderezar las cosas. Ya lo lograron en el pasado cuando cambiaron McLaren por Red Bull. Ahora tienen que tardar menos. De hecho, para tener un 2027 competitivo no valdría con un salto de 20 CV, van a necesitar unos 50, y que le magia de Newey haga el resto. En la escudería de la bebida energética ganaban carreras sin el mejor motor de la parrilla. Alonso, el gigante escondido de la Fórmula 1, está convencido de tener todos los mimbres para regresar al podio.

articles.title: Fernando Alonso, renovación con motivos... y una gran duda
articles.standfirst: El asturiano seguirá en la F1 con una ampliación multianual de su vinculación con Aston Martin tras varios meses de incertidumbre total
articles.summary: El asturiano seguirá en la F1 con una ampliación multianual de su vinculación con Aston Martin tras varios meses de incertidumbre total
articles.body: El momento llegó tras meses de espera y varias carreras con mensajes contradictorios: Aston Martin anunciaba que Fernando Alonso seguirá siendo su piloto en la Fórmula 1. Lo hizo jugando, de alguna forma, con el tono de toda la temporada. "Me retiraré... pero no ahora", comunicó en sus redes sociales. Pero es la confirmación de su ampliación multianual, tal y como se hacen con las negociaciones actuales, permitiendo que amplíe su carrera deportiva más allá de los 440 Grandes Premios. Por encima de todo lo demás, dos campeonatos y el sueño final de un tercero que rozó en 2007, 2010 o 2012. La renovación de Alonso no fue un asunto sencillo. En la mesa de negociación había aspectos clave como las sensaciones del piloto con la nueva reglamentación del deporte, el rendimiento deportivo de su proyecto y una relación con el equipo que pasa por un sueldo de estrella, el papel más allá de las carreras o los proyectos que el piloto quiere realizar más allá de la F1.Existen motivos de peso, aunque también dudas razonables. "Seguimos con la ambición de ser campeones del mundo", adelantó su gran jefe, Lawrence Stroll, como carta de presentación. Palabras mayores. El rendimiento deportivo es el elemento a partir de lo que se sustenta todo lo demás. Si bien es cierto que el piloto quiere una F1 que le llene, nada se entendería sin un proyecto a la altura. Aston no lo está este año, pero el asturiano cree que llegarán: "Hay un chasis que sobresale, para el motor debemos esperar". Defiende como argumento principal la capacidad de de desarrollo de la fábrica, el lápiz de Newey y da a Honda una vida extra. La teoría dice que no llegarán en 2027, pero desde el equipo verde y la firma japonesa presionan a la FIA para obtener algún tipo de ventaja. En el medio, espera a una F1 con cambios a mejor. El piloto ha defendido que estos coches van contra el instinto de piloto y ha repetido que su obligación con el deporte es buscar una mejor competición. "Renueve o no, la F1 no puede seguir así", lanzó en Madrid. En 2027 habrá un ajuste hacia el 60/40 en la potencia del motor de combustión y la energía, y en el horizonte de 2030 aparecen los V8. Alonso, al mismo tiempo, sabe que su nivel no ha disminuido. Ya en este 2026 ha obtenido tres puntos de la nada con coches mucho más rápidos detrás y en su carrera con Aston jamás ha bajado del top-10 de la clasificación. Claro que tras ese 2023 de los ocho podios la historia parecía diferente. La renovación también atiende un condicionante económico. No existe el valor concreto de su ampliación, pero en la nueva F1 se han disparado los sueldos gracias a los nuevos valores de mercado, patrocinios y creciente valor de las fábricas. Por ejemplo, el contrato de Max Verstappen pasa de los 90 millones por curso, Lewis Hamilton está en los 70 y Carlos Sainz, por ejemplo, firmó por unos 30 con Williams. En el caso del ovetense, nada hace indicar que los nuevos guarismos de un bicampeón en un equipo pujante se quede lejos de esos valores, con una cifra estimada en unos 40 o 50 por el especialista Marc Limacher. Es un añadido clave. Al mismo tiempo, en Aston Martin también encuentra una gran libertad de movimientos. El bicampeón tenía la sartén por el mango a la hora de decidir qué haría con su futuro, y sabía que seguiría vinculado al proyecto deportivo de alguna u otra forma. Eso no cambiará y le permitirá abrir miras si no sale bien su nuevo intento dentro de la clase reina. Las 24 Horas de Le Mans, la triple corona con las 500 Millas de Indianápolis o el Rally Dakar siguen ahí presentes. Aunque ya no tan cerca. Pero si existe una pregunta por encima de las demás tiene que ver con las opciones reales futuras del piloto asturiano en la Fórmula 1. Muy pocas veces (BrawnGP en 2009 o McLaren entre 2023 y 2024 son las más recientes) se ha visto a un equipo pasar del fondo de la tabla a lo más alto, y suena realmente complicado pensar en un gran salto del proyecto verde en el corto plazo. Más si cabe en un reglamento de motores. Honda, no es novedad, va a contrapié y debe volver a lo más alto en un tiempo récord. En la época de McLaren y después Red Bull pasó casi cinco años para conseguir una unidad de potencia vencedora y quizá es un tiempo que el asturiano no tiene. O sí, pero dependerá de su paciencia. "No puedo esperar otra vez cinco años", decía durante este año. Presión, en toda regla. Pero hay otra vertiente, más positiva. Tiene que ver con el éxito de su fábrica para acometer y completar las primeras mejoras, con una idea de Newey convertida en realidad. El chasis ya enseñó que Aston, entre túnel de viento y fábrica, tiene mimbres para construir y es algo que sus pilotos conocen. "Creo de verdad en lo que estamos construyendo: tenemos un liderazgo fuerte, gente increíble, compañeros e instalaciones", cerró la estrella tras su flamante renovación.

articles.title: Madison Beer gushes over 'incredible' Justin Herbert, WAG culture is headed to college & the NASCAR swear jar
articles.summary: Madison Beer gushed about her engagement to Justin Herbert on Twitch, calling the proposal "magical" despite the Chargers' rough 0-3 season.
articles.body: 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com. Happy Tuesday, friends. I am thrilled to be back in the beautiful state of Tennessee. Where have I been, you ask? Let me tell ya. This weekend, I traveled to majestic Branson, Missouri. Or as I like to call it, Pigeon Forge Jr. (IYKYK). CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I got the invite to check out the SMX (that's supermotocross for the uncultured) World Championship Final and the YETI Open on Table Rock Lake. Now, if you've never been to Branson, let me paint you a picture: kitschy stores, celebrity chain restaurants and dinner theaters. Oh, and pretty much the whole town is owned by Bass Pro Shops. But the scenery in this particular slice of the country is also stunning. Rolling hills, a big, beautiful lake, an outdoorsman's paradise. Hence, the Bass Pro Shops thing. Anyway, on Sunday I had the honor of going fishing with none other than Bassmaster Elite Pro Cooper Gallant. I'll admit I'm a pretty hopeless bass angler. But who better to teach me than someone who does it for a living? So if you're into that sort of thing (that "thing" being bagging largies) stay tuned to OutKick OutDoors. Make sure you're subscribed on YouTube and following on Instagram and TikTok. Otherwise, you might miss the absolute leviathan (not pictured) that I caught while we were out there. And that would be a real shame for you. With that out of the way, let's get on to some Nightcaps, shall we? College football WAGs are apparently a thing now WAG culture has gotten completely out of control. Look, I know — we love WAGs here at OutKick. It's become a whole genre, especially in 'Caps. But once the NFL started using the WAGs to "market to women," the whole thing just became a little too... forced? And now, apparently, the college girls are getting in on it. Meet Allison Kaye, a makeup artist whose entire business is traveling around the country getting athletes' wives and girlfriends glammed up for game day. She started with NFL WAGs, but this season, she's taking "Game Day Glam" to college campuses. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! She started at Ohio State earlier this month, doing makeup for four players' girlfriends. Then she went to Penn State and did six more. And I have to say, this woman has found herself one hell of a business model. She doesn't just show up with a Caboodle (remember those?), either. She turns her hotel room into a whole "glam suite" with food, drinks, team decorations and free stuff from beauty brands. The girlfriends pay for the service themselves. Or with their boyfriends' NIL money. Apparently, her weekends are now almost completely booked for the rest of football season. There are 134 FBS football teams, approximately one bazillion players and, presumably, a whole lot of girlfriends who would rather not do their own makeup at 7 a.m. before a noon kickoff. I don't know what Allison Kaye is charging for this, but I do know she might have stumbled upon a gold mine. Maybe I should learn how to use a curling iron. Get a little side hustle going. Speaking of WAGS... Madison Beer is positively gushing over Justin Herbert You know who could use a win right now? Justin Herbert. The Chargers are 0-3. Their offense STINKS. And every day he has to go to work and listen to Mike McDaniel say things like "we're not standing on business" in his rolled up joggers. But you know what Justin Herbert does have? Madison Beer. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER And Madison Beer is apparently VERY into Justin Herbert. The singer recently hopped on Twitch and talked about their July engagement, which she described as "magical." She also said the proposal happened exactly one year after Herbert asked her to be his girlfriend and gushed about how lucky she feels to have found him. So sure, things at work aren't going great for Herbs. But at the end of the day, he gets to go home to Madison Beer, who is hot, wildly successful and seemingly thinks he hung the moon. No matter what those insufferable dorks over on the "Speakeasy" podcast have to say about her. No mailbag today (womp) because my email inbox is bone dry (minus about 100 irrelevant PR pitches). Let's remedy this for next week. 📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.) 🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding 📸 Instagram: @amberharding One more thing: NASCAR's swear jar If you've ever screamed obscenities after getting cut off on the interstate or just while sitting in traffic in general, you can probably imagine the colorful language that gets thrown around during NASCAR races. And not just during the post-race fistfights, either. Anyway, the potty mouths are so bad that NASCAR has implemented a swear jar, and they are keeping a running tally of which expletives get used the most. You'll never guess which four-letter word tops the leaderboard. (Yes you will.)
